vignette:
Detective Marcus: The Weight of Old Wounds

Marcus is a fifty-six-year-old detective with the city police department, a man whose career has been built on his ability to read people, to notice what others miss, to stay calm under pressure. He carries himself with the measured confidence of someone who has spent three decades in law enforcement, though lately there's a wariness to him, a tension in his shoulders that doesn't quite release even when he's sitting in the quiet of the therapy office.

His childhood was spent in a home where his father's temper was the weather—unpredictable, violent, and inescapable. Marcus remembers the sound of his father's belt being pulled from its loops, the way his mother would go very still at the dinner table, the particular quality of silence that meant something was coming. His father used his hands too, used his voice, used whatever was within reach. By the time Marcus was twelve, he had learned to make himself small, to anticipate rage the way other children anticipate Christmas.

He joined the police force at twenty-three, driven by something he couldn't quite name then—a need to be the one in control, to be the one with authority, to ensure that people like his father couldn't hurt people like his younger self. For decades, this worked. The structure of the job, the clear hierarchy, the rules that applied equally—these things made sense to him. He was good at his work. He made detective by thirty-five. His colleagues respected him.

But the trauma doesn't stay buried just because you've built a life on top of it.

About eighteen months ago, Marcus was investigating a case involving a child who had been abused by a parent. The details were graphic—the kind of details that accumulate in a detective's mind whether you want them there or not. That night, Marcus went home to his apartment and found himself on the kitchen floor at three in the morning, his body shaking in a way he couldn't control. He couldn't remember getting there. He couldn't remember if he'd been drinking. The memory of his father's face kept appearing unbidden, overlapping with the face of the man he'd arrested that day.

Since then, Marcus has been caught in a cycle he doesn't know how to escape. He has nightmares most nights—visceral, physical things where he wakes gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs. He's stopped going to the precinct gym because being in that space makes him hypervigilant, scanning for threats that aren't there. He finds himself getting angry at small things—a coworker's tone of voice, a driver cutting him off—and the anger is disproportionate, explosive in a way that frightens him because it reminds him of his father.

His ex-wife used to tell him he was emotionally unavailable, that he couldn't let anyone close. She was right, though he couldn't have articulated why then. Now he understands that intimacy meant vulnerability, and vulnerability meant danger. The divorce was finalized five years ago, and he hasn't attempted another relationship.

Marcus avoids cases involving child abuse now, which means avoiding conversations with his captain about why. He's started taking extra shifts, staying late at the station where the work is straightforward and the danger is external. He drinks more than he used to, though he wouldn't call it a problem. He just knows that without it, the evenings are too long, too quiet, too full of the echoes of a childhood he can't seem to outrun.

He sits in the therapy office now, a man in the middle of his life, still waiting for the safety he thought he'd earned.
